newsitem.title: GERMANY: Flood land in east Germany must be drained.
newsitem.headline: Flood land in east Germany must be drained.

text.p: Soldiers and relief workers will soon start draining large tracts of farmland along Germany's eastern border that were flooded last month, authorities said on Monday.

Six villages were partially or totally submerged almost to the rooftops, about 7,200 hectares (18,000 acres) were inundated and 300 residents were evacuated from the Ziltendorf basin when a flood barrier broke there last month.

Despite retreating water levels on the River Oder, flood water was not draining away by itself and would have to be pumped out, Brandenburg state environment minister Matthias Platzeck told Berlin's InfoRadio.
Three weeks of the worst flooding in living memory in the region has devastated large tracts of farmland, ruined crops and wrecked villages.

The total damage has yet to be calculated, but officials fear it could run in to billions of marks. Germany has, however, escaped the worst of the floods which killed more than 100 people in the neighbouring Czech Republic and Poland.

"We hope to start building a secondary dam in the next few days where the big dike breach took place near (the village of) Aurith so that we can dry the area near the main dam itself and begin repair work," Platzeck said.
Platzeck's ministry said it would cost at least 132 million marks ($70 million) to repair damaged dikes along the river which forms part of Germany's border with Poland.

Record high river water levels had completely destroyed 3,500 metres (yards) of the 160-km (100-mile) flood barriers, about five km (three miles) of the dikes will need repairs and 28 km (16 miles) of dike paths will have to be rebuilt, the ministry said.
But German environmental group BUND criticised the authorities' plans to regenerate the flooded area, saying they should let the river run its natural course.
BUND flood expert Sebastian Schoenauer said the river had lost 80 percent of its original spillage area to settlements and farmland.
This, combined with unusally heavy rain storms in the Czech Republic and Poland, caused the region's worst deluge in centuries.
Schoenauer called on the European Union to set aside money to fund the closure of businesses and farms in the area. ($ = 1.849 German Marks)
